hero.title: Local Government: Panchayati Raj
hero.description: Master the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992—including the historical committees, Gram Sabha, three-tier structure, Article 243-A to 243-O, mandatory vs. voluntary provisions, State Finance Commission, State Election Commission, and the PESA Act, 1996 (UPSC GS Paper-II: Indian Polity).

timeline.title: Historical Evolution of Panchayati Raj
timeline.description: Chronology of committees and constitutional development leading to the enactment of the 73rd Amendment.

cards.details: Recommended a 3-tier Panchayati Raj system with democratic decentralization. Resulted in Rajasthan (Nagaur district) becoming the first state to establish Panchayats in 1959.
Recommended replacing the 3-tier system with a 2-tier system (Mandal Panchayat and Zilla Parishad) and suggested official participation of political parties.
Appointed by the Planning Commission. Concluded that the development administration had become bureaucratic, calling PRIs 'grass without roots'.
Singhvi Committee recommended constitutional recognition for PRIs to ensure regular, free, and fair elections, leading to the drafting of constitutional amendment bills.

mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Quick tools to memorize the chronology of committees and core Articles.

items.title: Mnemonic 1
items.decryption: Chronological order: Balwant Rai Mehta (1957) → Ashok Mehta (1977) → G.V.K. Rao (1985) → Singhvi Committee (1986).

items.title: Mnemonic 2
items.decryption: Remember E is for Expiry or End of tenure, matching the 5-year duration of Panchayats.

items.title: Mnemonic 3
items.decryption: Remember F is for Failure to qualify or Fines/disqualifications of members.

items.title: Mnemonic 4
items.decryption: Remember I stands for Income/Finance (State Finance Commission) and K stands for Kicking off elections (State Election Commission).

flashcards.title: Active Recall Flashcards
flashcards.description: Active-recall review of constitutional requirements and PESA.

items.question: Is the establishment of a Gram Sabha mandatory under the 73rd Amendment?
items.answer: Yes. Under Article 243A, the establishment of a Gram Sabha (consisting of all registered voters in the village area) is a mandatory provision.

items.question: What is the minimum age required to contest elections to a Panchayat?
items.answer: A candidate must have completed the age of 21 years (Article 243F), which is lower than the 25-year limit for state legislative assembly elections.

items.question: What is the mandatory reservation quota for women in Panchayats?
items.answer: Not less than one-third (33%) of the total number of seats (including seats reserved for SCs/STs) and offices of chairpersons must be reserved for women (Article 243D). Some states have voluntarily increased this to 50%.

items.question: Are Panchayats exempted from constitutional status in states with population under 20 lakhs?
items.answer: No, they still get constitutional status. However, states with a population under 20 lakhs have the option to NOT constitute Panchayats at the intermediate (block) level (Article 243B).

items.question: What is the primary objective of the PESA Act, 1996?
items.answer: The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act (PESA) extends Part IX of the Constitution to Scheduled areas (Fifth Schedule) with modifications, empowering Gram Sabhas to safeguard tribal customs, manage minor forest produce, and approve land acquisition.

traps.title: UPSC Civil Services Exam Traps to Avoid
items: Trap 1: Believing that reservation of seats for Backward Classes (OBCs) is mandatory. No! Reservation for SCs and STs is compulsory based on their population proportion, but reservation for OBCs is a voluntary (discretionary) provision left to state legislatures.

Trap 2: Assuming the State Election Commissioner (SEC) can be removed at the pleasure of the Governor. No! Although appointed by the Governor, the SEC can only be removed in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Judge of a High Court, ensuring independence.

Trap 3: Confusing the authority of the State Finance Commission (SFC). The SFC is appointed by the Governor under Article 243-I every 5 years, and it reviews the financial position of both Panchayats and Municipalities (under Article 243-Y) and recommends tax distribution.

sections.title: 1. Committee Milestones & PRI Evolution
sections.content:
Democratic Decentralization Evolution

Panchayati Raj was recommended in 1957 to secure popular participation in community projects. Despite establishment, early PRIs failed due to irregular elections, lack of finances, and administrative apathy. The L.M. Singhvi Committee in 1986 first argued that constitutionalization was essential to protect local bodies from political interference.

sections.title: 2. 73rd Amendment PRI Structure & Provisions
sections.content:
Mandatory vs. Voluntary Framework

Part IX of the Constitution contains two sets of provisions: (1) Mandatory (Compulsory) provisions which all states must adopt (like establishing Gram Sabha, 3-tier structure, reservation for SCs/STs/women, and setting up SFC/SEC), and (2) Voluntary (Discretionary) provisions which states may adopt at their own discretion (like giving voting rights to MPs/MLAs in Panchayats, representation of OBCs, and devolution of financial powers).

Compulsory Provisions (Mandatory)Voluntary Provisions (Discretionary)
Organization of Gram Sabha in a village.Providing representation to MPs/MLAs in Panchayats.
Establishment of three-tier structure (except small states).Providing reservation of seats for backward classes (OBCs).
Direct election to all seats at all levels.Devolution of powers and functions under the 11th Schedule (29 matters).
33% reservation for women; SC/ST based on population.Granting financial powers to levy and collect taxes, duties, tolls.

sections.title: 3. PESA Act, 1996 & Financial Autonomy
sections.content:
PESA Act, 1996 (Extension Act)

PESA extends Part IX to the Scheduled Areas (Fifth Schedule) in 10 states. It vests significant powers in the Gram Sabha rather than the higher tiers, acknowledging tribal self-rule. Gram Sabhas have the power of mandatory consultation before land acquisition, ownership of minor forest produce, power to prevent land alienation, and control over local plans and resources.

Financial Devolution & Audits

Panchayats rely heavily on: (1) Grants-in-aid from the State and Central government (under recommendations of SFC and Central Finance Commission), and (2) State tax sharing. Under Article 243H, state legislatures may authorize Panchayats to levy taxes, fees, and tolls to build self-reliance.
